chapter.name: Large Numbers Around Us
chapter.blurb: Reading/writing large numbers (lakh, crore, arab), Indian vs American naming, rounding, estimation, and multiplication shortcuts.

scope: Read and write numbers up to crores/arabs in the Indian place-value system, with correct comma placement
Build a number as a sum of place-value multiples in more than one way; find the fewest-click (minimal) representation
Convert a number between the Indian (lakh/crore/arab) and American (thousand/million/billion) naming systems
Round a number up or down appropriately for a stated everyday context
Find the nearest thousand/lakh/crore of a number; estimate whether a sum or difference exceeds a stated round value
Use factor regrouping (e.g. x5 = x10/2, x25 = x100/4) to multiply quickly
Predict the number of digits in a product from the digit-counts of its factors
Answer a real-world large-number estimation question using staged multiplication/division and reasonable assumptions
Use 1,00,000 as the smallest 6-digit number, compare a lifetime in days (365 x years) with one lakh, and say how much more or less than a lakh a given population is
Get a feel for a large quantity by comparing it with a familiar one, and argue whether a lakh is big or small depending on what it is compared with
Relate lakh, crore and arab (1 lakh = 100 thousand, 1 crore = 100 lakh, 1 arab = 100 crore) and count the zeros in each
Solve digit-arrangement puzzles with a 10-digit number that uses each digit once, and write calculator button-click expressions such as 92,100 = 9 x 10,000 + 21 x 100
Solve toothpick-digit puzzles: count the sticks in a number and make bigger or smaller numbers with a given number of sticks

concepts.name: Reading & writing large numbers (Indian system)
concepts.description: Placing commas and naming numbers up to crores/arabs using the Indian place-value system.
concepts.idea: Indian commas group digits 3-2-2-2 from the right (thousand, lakh, crore, arab), unlike the uniform 3-3-3 American grouping.
concepts.rule: 100 thousand = 1 lakh; 100 lakh = 1 crore; 100 crore = 1 arab.
concepts.example: 12,78,830 = twelve lakh seventy eight thousand eight hundred thirty.

concepts.name: Indian vs. American/International numbering systems
concepts.description: Converting a number between Indian naming (lakh, crore, arab) and American naming (thousand, million, billion).
concepts.idea: The same number has two different names and comma placements depending on the system.
concepts.rule: 10 lakh = 1 million; 1 crore = 10 million; 1 arab = 1 billion.

concepts.name: Place-value composition & minimal representations
concepts.description: Building a number as a sum of place-value multiples in more than one way, and finding the representation using the fewest terms.
concepts.idea: Any number can be built from multiples of 1, 10, 100, 1000... in several combinations.
concepts.rule: The fewest-click representation is the one that matches the number's own Indian place-value digits.

concepts.name: Rounding large numbers
concepts.description: Rounding a number up or down to a stated context, and finding the nearest thousand / lakh / crore of a given number.
concepts.idea: An approximation is often more useful than an exact count for everyday communication.
concepts.rule: Round up when the approximation must not fall short; round down when it must not overshoot.

concepts.name: Estimating sums and differences of large numbers
concepts.description: Judging whether an estimated sum/difference is greater or less than a stated round value, without computing the exact value first.
concepts.idea: Estimation before exact calculation catches errors and builds number sense.
concepts.rule: Compare each number to its nearest round neighbour to bound the sum/difference before computing exactly.

concepts.name: Multiplication shortcuts via regrouping
concepts.description: Rewriting a product using an equivalent factor (e.g. 5 = 10/2, 25 = 100/4, 125 = 1000/8) to calculate mentally.
concepts.idea: Multiplying by 5, 25, 125, 50, 250 etc. is quicker via a related power of 10.
concepts.rule: a x 5 = a x 10 / 2 (and similarly for 25, 125, 50...).

concepts.name: Digit-count patterns in products
concepts.description: Predicting the number of digits in a product of two numbers from the number of digits in the factors, without multiplying.
concepts.idea: The smallest and largest possible products for given digit-lengths bound the digit-count of any product of that shape.
concepts.rule: An m-digit x n-digit product has either (m+n-1) or (m+n) digits.
concepts.example: A 2-digit x 2-digit product is always a 3- or 4-digit number.

concepts.name: Real-world estimation with large numbers
concepts.description: Using reasonable assumptions and staged multiplication/division to answer a Fermi-style real-world question involving large quantities.
concepts.idea: Large real-world questions are answered by breaking them into stages with sensible assumptions.
concepts.rule: Convert a rate (per day/per second) to a total by multiplying by the relevant count, computing in stages.
concepts.example: At 100 km/day, distance in 10 years = 100 x 365 x 10 km, computed in stages.

concepts.name: Lakh, crore and arab in context
concepts.description: How lakh, crore and arab relate to each other and to thousands, how many zeros each has, and how to judge and compare the size of a lakh using everyday quantities.
concepts.idea: Each Indian unit is 100 times the one before it, so the number of zeros grows by two each time from a lakh to a crore to an arab.
concepts.rule: 1 lakh = 100 thousand (5 zeros); 1 crore = 100 lakh (7 zeros); 1 arab = 100 crore (9 zeros); a thousand lakh is 10 crore (8 zeros); 99,999 + 1 = 1,00,000.
concepts.example: 365 x 100 = 36,500 days in 100 years, so 3 varieties a day gives 3 x 36,500 = 1,09,500, which is more than one lakh.

concepts.name: Large-number puzzles: digit arrangements and toothpick digits
concepts.description: Puzzle-style problems: arranging the digits 0 to 9 into the largest or smallest number, button-click expressions on a two-button calculator, writing numbers in a row, and counting sticks in toothpick digits.
concepts.idea: To make the largest or smallest number, place the biggest or smallest digits in the highest places first, subject to the condition given (for example an even last digit).
concepts.rule: A number is a multiple of 5 only if it ends in 0 or 5, and even only if it ends in an even digit; a calculator with +10,000 and +100 can only show multiples of 100; more digits means a bigger number.
concepts.example: The largest 10-digit multiple of 5 that uses every digit once is 9876543210.
